title: Kyocera AVX Components Corp. v. United States
articleTitle: An In-Depth Analysis of Kyocera AVX Components Corp. v. United States: A Paradigm Shift in Research and Development Tax Credit Substantiation and Corporate Compliance
court: United States Court of Federal Claims
subject: Qualified Research Expenses
summary: Evaluated whether certain expenses, such as production materials, qualified as QREs or were merely routine manufacturing costs.

body.text: The federal research and development tax credit, established under Section 41 of the Internal Revenue Code, has long been a cornerstone of American industrial policy, designed to foster innovation by lowering the after-tax cost of technological advancement. However, the application of this credit has increasingly become a flashpoint for litigation between multinational corporations and the Internal Revenue Service. At the vanguard of this conflict is the case of Kyocera AVX Components Corp. v. United States, a complex and evolving legal battle that serves as a critical bellwether for the future of R&D tax substantiation. The dispute, which spans multiple tax years and judicial forums, highlights a fundamental shift in the government's approach to tax audits: a move away from the acceptance of retrospective estimates and toward a mandate for granular, contemporaneous, and system-generated documentation. For corporate tax teams and their advisors, the Kyocera AVX litigation represents a cautionary tale of how inadequate recordkeeping can transform a legitimate refund claim into a multi-million-dollar liability.
The Regulatory Foundation and the Evolution of the Four-Part Test

To evaluate the significance of the Kyocera AVX dispute, one must first examine the statutory requirements that govern the Section 41 credit. The credit is available only for "qualified research expenses," which are defined as costs incurred for "qualified research" conducted by the taxpayer. The determination of what constitutes qualified research is governed by a rigorous "four-part test," each element of which must be satisfied for every business component for which a credit is claimed.

The first requirement is the Section 174 Test, which dictates that expenditures must be deductible under Section 174 of the Internal Revenue Code. This means the costs must be incurred in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business and must represent research and development costs in the experimental or laboratory sense. The second requirement is the Technological in Nature Test, which mandates that the research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature, relying on principles of physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. The third requirement, the Business Component Test, requires that the research be intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component, defined as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in its trade or business.

The fourth and most frequently litigated requirement is the Process of Experimentation Test. Under this test, substantially all of the activities of the research must constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a purpose related to a new or improved function, performance, or reliability or quality. A process of experimentation involves the identification of uncertainty regarding the capability or method for achieving a desired result, or the appropriate design of that result, followed by the systematic evaluation of one or more alternatives to resolve that uncertainty. The term "substantially all" is generally interpreted by the courts and the Internal Revenue Service as meaning that at least 80 percent of the research activities, measured on a business component basis, must constitute elements of a process of experimentation.

This "substantially all" threshold is often the primary point of failure for taxpayers who lack detailed time tracking. As demonstrated in recent jurisprudence, the Internal Revenue Service and the courts have increasingly applied a strict fractional analysis to this requirement. The "substantially all" fraction can be expressed as:
$$Substantially\ All\ Fraction = \frac{Activities\ constituting\ a\ process\ of\ experimentation}{Total\ activities\ related\ to\ the\ business\ component} \ge 0.80$$

In the absence of contemporaneous records, taxpayers find it nearly impossible to provide a principled basis for this calculation, a vulnerability that was central to the government's motion in the Kyocera AVX case.
The Corporate Context: Kyocera AVX and the Electronics Manufacturing Sector

Kyocera AVX Components Corporation, formerly known as AVX Corporation before becoming a wholly-owned subsidiary of Kyocera Corporation in 2020, is a global leader in the manufacturing of advanced electronic components. The company’s product portfolio includes multilayer ceramic capacitors (MLCCs), tantalum capacitors, antennas, microwave filters, and integrated electronic control units (ECUs) used in high-growth markets such as 5G telecommunications, the Internet of Things (IoT), and advanced driver-assistance systems (ADAS) in the automotive sector.

The manufacturing of these components involves extreme technical complexity and high-stakes engineering. For example, the development of small, high-capacitance ceramic capacitors requires resolving significant uncertainties related to material reliability under varying temperature and humidity conditions. Similarly, the design of large-sized multilayer packages for high-speed signals involves optimizing wideband memory connections to support large-capacity data transmission. Given the inherent technological nature of these activities, Kyocera AVX has historically been a significant claimant of the Section 41 R&D tax credit.

The current dispute originated when Kyocera AVX sought to optimize its tax position by filing amended returns for the tax years 2017 through 2020. For the 2018 tax year, the company had originally claimed an R&D credit of $398,985. Following a comprehensive study conducted by the professional services firm PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC), the company filed an amended return seeking to increase the 2018 credit to approximately $1.7 million—an increase of more than $1.3 million. This significant escalation in the claimed credit, based on a retrospective study, drew immediate scrutiny from the Internal Revenue Service and set the stage for one of the most consequential R&D tax cases of the decade.
Comparative Financial Claims and the Escalation of Litigation

The financial stakes in the Kyocera AVX litigation have grown exponentially since the initial filing of the amended return. What began as a dispute over a $1.3 million refund has evolved into a multi-front legal battle involving over $20 million in potential credits, refunds, and deficiencies. The following table outlines the primary financial elements of the dispute as of early 2025.

body.text: The escalation of the government's claims highlights a critical strategic risk for taxpayers: the filing of an amended return for additional credits can serve as a catalyst for a full-scale audit of the taxpayer's original filings. In Kyocera AVX's case, the pursuit of an additional $1.3 million in credits resulted in the Internal Revenue Service questioning a previous $13.36 million refund, transforming a refund claim into a defensive struggle for the company’s financial stability.
Critical Analysis of the PwC Study and Documentation Failures

The heart of the government's successful motion for summary judgment in the District Court centered on the methodology of the R&D study performed by PwC. The study relied almost entirely on a traditional "look-back" approach, which utilized retrospective interviews with 36 subject matter experts (SMEs) to represent and allocate the research activities of approximately 1,200 employees. This method, while common in the industry for decades, was deemed fundamentally insufficient by the court and the Internal Revenue Service under modern standards of proof.

The primary deficiency identified by the government was the lack of contemporaneous time tracking. Kyocera AVX did not maintain a centralized system that linked employee hours to specific research projects or business components during the years in question. Instead, the PwC study asked SMEs to provide percentage-based estimates of time spent on R&D activities long after the work was completed. The Internal Revenue Service argued that these estimates were arbitrary and lacked the "activity-level evidence" necessary to prove that "substantially all" of the activities for each business component constituted a process of experimentation.

Furthermore, the litigation revealed a significant procedural failure: neither Kyocera AVX nor PwC was able to produce the original survey responses or the underlying interview materials during the discovery process. The government was particularly critical of PwC's recordkeeping, noting that the firm failed to retain the primary documents generated during its own study. This failure to maintain and produce primary evidence was seen as a violation of basic recordkeeping requirements and led the court to conclude that the taxpayer could not meet its burden of proof as a matter of law.

The rejection of the PwC study reinforces a growing trend in tax litigation: the professional reputation of a Big Four accounting firm is no longer sufficient to shield a taxpayer from the necessity of providing primary, contemporaneous documentation. As the Internal Revenue Service has explicitly stated, oral testimony and retrospective interviews should be used for "filling the potholes," not for "paving the road" of a research credit claim.
The Procedural Shift: Jurisdiction and the Move to Tax Court

A significant development in the Kyocera AVX litigation occurred in early 2025 when the procedural focus shifted from the District Court to the U.S. Tax Court. Initially, Kyocera AVX had filed a refund suit in the U.S. District Court for the District of South Carolina, seeking the recovery of the denied $1.3 million amended credit. However, as the dispute expanded to include the government's countersuit for the return of a $13.36 million refund and the company’s contest of a new $2.3 million deficiency assessment, the jurisdictional landscape changed.

In March 2025, a district judge in South Carolina ruled that the issues being disputed by Kyocera AVX and the Internal Revenue Service fell under the exclusive jurisdiction of the Tax Court. This dismissal of the District Court case without prejudice meant that all the primary legal questions—including the validity of the R&D documentation and the appropriateness of the previous refunds—would be resolved in a single, specialized forum. This move to the Tax Court is significant because the Tax Court is uniquely positioned to handle complex technical and accounting disputes and often applies a highly rigorous standard to documentation requirements in Section 41 cases.

The jurisdictional shift also highlights the "multi-million-dollar nightmare" Kyocera AVX faces, as the company must now fight on multiple fronts to defend its previous tax positions while simultaneously pursuing its refund claims. The potential for a "worst-case scenario" exists where Kyocera AVX not only fails to secure the $7 million in sought credits (R&D plus Section 965) but is also forced to repay over $13 million to the government.
Precedential Context: Little Sandy Coal and Park-Ohio

The Kyocera AVX litigation does not exist in isolation; it is deeply intertwined with other recent landmark cases that have redefined the R&D credit landscape. Most notably, the Internal Revenue Service and the courts have relied heavily on the precedent established in Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner.

In the Little Sandy Coal case, which involved a shipbuilder claiming credits for the development of "first-in-class" vessels, the Seventh Circuit Court of Appeals affirmed a Tax Court ruling that documentation on time spent on specific activities was a mandatory prerequisite for qualifying for Section 41 refunds. The court in Little Sandy Coal rejected the "novelty argument"—the idea that because an entire product is new, all activities associated with its production are experimental. Instead, the court emphasized that the Section 41 test must be applied in reference to specific activities, and the taxpayer must provide a "principled way" to determine what portion of employee time constituted a process of experimentation. The Kyocera AVX court explicitly cited Little Sandy Coal when it moved to dismiss the company’s amended claim, signaling that the "principled way" requirement is now a standard expectation for large-scale R&D claims.

Another critical companion case is Park-Ohio Holdings Corp. v. United States, filed in the Northern District of Ohio in early 2025. The Park-Ohio case challenges the Internal Revenue Service's new, highly granular requirements for filing R&D refund claims. Under procedures implemented in 2022, the Internal Revenue Service will not even process an R&D refund claim unless it is accompanied by an "incredible amount of granular and detailed information" regarding each business component and the specific research activities performed. Park-Ohio has argued that these requirements are "arbitrary and capricious" and were implemented in violation of the Administrative Procedure Act. The resolution of Park-Ohio will determine the procedural barriers taxpayers face when filing for refunds, while the Kyocera AVX case determines the evidentiary standard those claims must meet to survive an audit or litigation.
Technological Implications and the Move to Automated Time Tracking

One of the most profound implications of the Kyocera AVX case for future R&D tax credit applications is the virtual mandate for automated time tracking and real-time documentation. The court’s rejection of SME interviews and retrospective estimates has effectively rendered traditional, manual "look-back" studies obsolete for large companies.

For manufacturing and engineering-intensive companies like Kyocera AVX, the path to compliance now requires the integration of tax requirements with existing project management and version control systems. Tools such as Jira, GitHub, Asana, and Monday.com are increasingly being leveraged to provide a contemporaneous, auditable trail of documentation. These systems generate metadata that is recorded "at the same time" as the technical work, satisfying the legal definition of contemporaneous documentation.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is also playing an increasingly central role in this transition. Advanced AI solutions can now ingest massive amounts of data from engineering systems and systematically identify which projects and activities meet the four-part test. By calculating time allocations directly from metadata, AI eliminates the need for intrusive SME interviews and the inherent errors associated with retrospective memory. The Kyocera AVX case serves as a powerful catalyst for this technological shift, demonstrating that the cost of modernizing R&D tracking systems is far lower than the potential cost of losing millions in tax credits due to inadequate documentation.
The Technical Challenges of Ceramic Capacitor Research

A nuanced understanding of the Kyocera AVX case requires a deep dive into the specific technological uncertainties the company’s engineering teams face. The production of multilayer ceramic capacitors (MLCCs) is not a static process; it is one of continuous miniaturization and performance enhancement. As electronic devices transition toward 5G and AI-enabled functionality, components must become smaller and more reliable.
Research in this field often involves a systematic process of experimentation to resolve uncertainties such as:

items: Material Reliability: Determining the appropriate ceramic and electrode materials that can maintain dielectric properties under extreme temperature and humidity variations without degradation or short-circuiting.

Manufacturing Scalability: Developing proprietary technologies to integrate electronics production expertise with high-volume manufacturing while maintaining tight tolerances for high-speed signal processing.

Signal Integrity: Resolving design uncertainties related to high-frequency signals and wideband memory connections in large-sized multilayer packages, which are critical for ADAS and millimeter-wave radar applications.

body.text: Each of these challenges requires a methodical plan to test alternatives—the hallmark of a "process of experimentation." However, the Kyocera AVX case demonstrates that simply performing this high-level research is not enough. The taxpayer must be able to link these technical challenges to specific employee time entries and provide technical artifacts—such as test results, design iterations, and laboratory notes—that document the resolution of these uncertainties in real-time.
Broader Litigation Context: Data Breaches and Environmental Liabilities

The Section 41 tax litigation is occurring alongside other significant legal challenges for Kyocera AVX, which contribute to the company’s overall regulatory and litigation burden. Between February and March 2023, Kyocera AVX experienced a significant cyberattack and data breach, which resulted in the theft of personally identifiable information (PII) belonging to current and former employees. This incident led to a consolidated class-action lawsuit, Dollar v. Kyocera AVX Components Corporation, alleging negligence and breach of fiduciary duty. Although the District Court of South Carolina dismissed the class action in early 2025 for lack of standing, the litigation consumed significant executive time and resources.

Simultaneously, Kyocera AVX has been involved in long-running environmental litigation related to the Olean Wellfield Superfund Site in New York. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has sought reimbursement from the company for costs associated with contaminated soil and groundwater remediation under the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act (CERCLA). These parallel legal battles emphasize the high degree of scrutiny to which multinational manufacturers are subjected and underscore the necessity for rigorous documentation across all aspects of corporate operations—from environmental compliance to tax credit substantiation.
Strategic Recommendations for Future R&D Tax Credit Compliance

The findings in Kyocera AVX v. United States provide a clear roadmap for how companies must evolve their R&D tax credit strategies to survive modern Internal Revenue Service audits. The following pillars of compliance have emerged as essential for any enterprise seeking to claim the Section 41 credit.
Establishing Contemporaneous Time Tracking Systems

The most critical takeaway from the Kyocera AVX case is that time tracking is no longer optional for large-scale R&D claims. Companies must implement systems that log employee time on a project-by-project or business component basis as the work occurs. These logs should clearly distinguish between qualified research and non-qualifying activities such as routine maintenance or post-production support. The use of automated "tagging" in project management software can ensure that research time is captured with minimal burden on the engineering staff.
Redefining the Role of Subject Matter Experts

Tax teams must shift from using SMEs as the primary source of time allocation data to using them as expert witnesses who validate and contextualize existing documentation. SMEs should be selected based on their first-hand knowledge of the research and should be trained to support their statements with specific technical artifacts. The practice of asking high-level managers to provide estimates for large groups of subordinates should be avoided, as it lacks the "direct supervision" nexus required by the courts.
Implementing Robust Record Retention Policies

The Kyocera AVX case highlighted the devastating impact of failing to retain primary research documents and study interview materials. Tax teams must work with IT and engineering departments to ensure that relevant emails, design logs, test plans, and project narratives are preserved for the duration of the statutory period. This is especially important for companies pursuing amended returns, as these claims are subjected to much higher levels of procedural rigor.
Defining Business Components with Granularity

Companies should avoid using broad or vague definitions for business components. Instead, they should define research targets at a granular level that allows for a clear mapping of technological uncertainty and the process of experimentation used to resolve it. This granularity is essential for satisfying the "substantially all" rule and for providing the Internal Revenue Service with the "activity-level" detail it now demands.
Conclusion: The Future of the Research Credit in the United States

The saga of Kyocera AVX Components Corp. v. United States marks the end of an era in which the Section 41 credit was largely the domain of accounting firms and retrospective estimation. The Internal Revenue Service has successfully redefined the standard of proof, requiring a level of operational rigor that many large companies have yet to achieve. As the dispute moves toward a final resolution in the Tax Court, its influence will be felt across every industry that relies on technological innovation, from semiconductor manufacturing to biotechnology.

The case serves as a definitive warning: in the modern audit environment, the quality of a taxpayer’s documentation is just as important as the quality of their research. Companies that invest in real-time, automated tracking and integrate their tax and engineering workflows will be well-positioned to defend the credits they have earned. Those that continue to rely on retrospective interviews and "look-back" studies will find their claims increasingly vulnerable to denial and their previous refunds at risk of clawback. Ultimately, the Kyocera AVX case is not just about a tax credit; it is about a new standard of corporate transparency and the necessity of documenting the systematic evaluation of alternatives that drives modern industrial progress.
